Column (3) absorbs sector-department-year fixed effects, so size coefficients compare wages across firm-size categories within the same sector, department, and year. Column (4) adds occupational-position controls to the sector-department-year specification. All columns use GEIH expansion weights and constrain the size premium to be the same across formality groups. Standard errors are clustered by sector-department cells. Significance levels: * $p<0.10$, ** $p<0.05$, *** $p<0.01$.}

{\fontsize{6.5}{7.5}\selectfont\raggedright Main rows are log contrasts relative to 11--19 workers within formality. Summary premiums instead use solo work. Same preferred controls and weights. Salaried workers include private, government, and domestic employees and day laborers. SEs cluster by sector-department (559 full-sample, 555 salaried clusters). Equality tests use the full covariance matrix. SEs in parentheses. * $p<0.10$, ** $p<0.05$, *** $p<0.01$.\par}
\note{Main rows report within-formality log-wage contrasts relative to 11--19 workers. Summary premiums use solo work as the reference and equal $100[\exp(b)-1]$. Each column pair comes from one size-by-formality regression with sex, age, age squared, education, occupational-position controls, sector-department-year fixed effects, and GEIH expansion weights. Salaried workers comprise private, government, and domestic employees and day laborers. The restricted sample excludes 66 additional singleton cells. Standard errors in parentheses use sector-department clustering, with $G=559$ clusters in the full sample and $G=555$ among employees. Equality tests compare the formal and informal 101+/solo log contrasts (two-sided $t$ test) and jointly compare all eight size contrasts relative to solo work (Wald $F$ test with eight numerator degrees of freedom). Both use the full coefficient covariance and $G-1$ denominator degrees of freedom. * $p<0.10$, ** $p<0.05$, *** $p<0.01$.}
\end{frame}

All other size assignments, observations, controls, and weights remain fixed. The $p$-values test whether the unrestricted categorical profiles from Equation~(3) lie on the specified quadratic. There are six restrictions per formality group and twelve jointly. Cluster-robust Wald statistics divided by the number of restrictions use an $F_{q,G-1}$ reference distribution. There are 559 sector-department clusters or 17 sector clusters. These are approximate tests, especially with only 17 clusters. The repeated percentages emphasize that changing clustering does not change point estimates. The value 150 is the baseline assignment, not an observed mean for 101+.\par}

{\fontsize{6.5}{7.5}\selectfont\raggedright Destination cells are defined by sector, department, occupational position, size, and formality. Panel A reports intended movers as a percentage of all workers. The absent-destination columns instead use intended movers as their denominator. Pooled counts use all estimation years. Panel B permits a move only when its destination meets the stated unweighted observation count. Otherwise the worker stays at origin. The all-worker income denominator is unchanged. \textit{None} means that no intended move qualifies, not that the estimated wage contrast is zero. For the joint selected-destination scenario, the 2025 $n\geq30$ column contains only formal moves. These thresholds check whether the destination category is represented in the sample. They do not establish that a transition is feasible or that origin and destination workers have the same characteristics.\par}
